entry.title: Migrating to integers and floats
entry.content:
Migrating to integers and floats

tramaj had one number type, a double. It now has two, an integer and a float, and nothing converts between them unless the template says so. The same change brings arithmetic, as nine named builtins.

Arithmetic is an addition: a host turns it on, and a template that does not use it is unaffected. The number split is not optional, and it changes what some existing templates and hosts produce. This page covers the split.

Who is affected

implementationnumber splitarithmeticinteger range
tramaj-purs, and tramaj-halogen, tramaj-cli and the playground built on ityesyes-(2^53 - 1) to 2^53 - 1
tramaj-hsyesyessigned 64-bit
tramaj-rs, tramaj-cli-rs, tramaj-js, tramaj-react, tramaj-py, tramaj-gonot yetnot yetnumbers are doubles

The PureScript and Haskell changes are on the main branch and in no release yet. A host that follows main as a git dependency gets them on its next update. The other four implementations still behave as before, and will change the same way when they get the split.

The changes at a glance

whatbeforenow
str of a whole-valued floatstr(1.0) is 1str(1.0) is 1.0
eq across the two typeseq(1, 1.0) is truefalse
lt, lte, gt, gte across the two typesgt(1.5, 0) is truea TypeMismatch
a JSON number in the contexta double, whatever its text3 is an integer, 3.0 and 3e0 are floats
an integer outside the rangerounded to the nearest doublerefused: a parse error as a literal, a TypeMismatch in the context
the object key "$term"an ordinary keyreserved, like "$sym" and "$type"
the type primitive number (v4)a primitivegone: int and float replace it

1. A whole-valued float is written with a fraction

A number keeps its type when it is written. An integer is written as its digits. A float always carries a fraction or an exponent, so a float with no fractional part gets .0:

valuebeforenow
111
1.011.0
1e5100000100000.0
1.51.51.5

This applies to str, to string interpolation, and to every number in the JSON an evaluation returns: text values, attribute values, action payloads, value slots, and an expression program’s result.

What to do. Look for float literals that are whole (1.0, 1e5) and for context numbers a producer writes with a fraction ("ratio": 2.0). Where the text matters and the value is a count, make it an integer: write the literal 100000, or have the producer write 2. An integer renders exactly as before.

A consumer that reads the output with an ordinary JSON parser sees the same numeric value for 3 and 3.0. Only a consumer that compares the output as text, or that decodes it back into a Node, sees the difference.

2. Comparisons do not mix the two types

eq never equates an integer with a float, and the four ordering comparisons take two integers or two floats:

eq(1, 1.0)         -- false, was true
gt($ctx.ratio, 0)  -- TypeMismatch when ratio is a float

The first of these is silent: a branch or a filter that compared a context number with a literal of the other type now takes the other arm.

What to do. Write the literal in the type of what it is compared with: gt($ctx.ratio, 0.0) for a float, eq($ctx.count, 0) for an integer.

When the template does not know which type its host sends, and the implementation has arithmetic turned on, normalize with one of the two conversions. Each accepts both types:

gt(real($ctx.ratio), 0.0)   -- real: the float nearest to its argument
eq(floor($ctx.count), 0)    -- floor: the largest integer not above it

3. A JSON number is typed by its text

A number in the context is read as the literal of the same text. With neither a fraction nor an exponent it is an integer; with either it is a float. So {"n": 3} and {"n": 3.0} are two different contexts.

Two things follow for a host.

The producer of the context decides the type. A serializer with a single number type writes the float 3.0 as 3, and the template then receives an integer. If a template needs a float from such a producer, it normalizes with real, as above.

The host’s JSON parser must keep the difference. JavaScript’s JSON.parse and Haskell’s aeson Value both lose it. The two implementations therefore ship their own JSON value, and their public API takes it in place of the previous one:

PureScriptHaskell
moduleTramaj.JsonTramaj.Json
replacesData.Argonaut.Core.JsonData.Aeson.Value
read textjsonParserjsonParser
write textstringifystringify
bridgenone: build values with fromInt, fromFloat, …fromAeson, toAeson

The Haskell bridge cannot recover what aeson dropped. fromAeson makes every whole number that fits 64 bits an integer, and toAeson gives the type up again. Read the JSON text with jsonParser when the difference matters.

Numbers that are not values are refused. An integer-form number outside the implementation’s integer range is not rounded any more: it is a parse error as a literal and a TypeMismatch in the context. So is a float too large for a double, such as 1e400. The context is checked whole before evaluation starts, so the error does not depend on whether the template reads that number. -0 and -0.0 are read as zero.

The integer range differs between the two implementations (see the table at the top). Inside -(2^53 - 1) to 2^53 - 1 they agree. A larger integer that the Haskell implementation emits is refused by the PureScript one.

4. "$term" is a reserved key

Over a symbol, an arithmetic builtin does not compute. It evaluates to a term, written as an object with the keys "$term" and "arguments". To keep that unambiguous, "$term" joins "$sym" and "$type" as a reserved key, whether or not arithmetic is turned on:

  • an object literal with the key "$term" in a template is a parse error;
  • a context that carries the key is a TypeMismatch. The one exception is a well-formed term seeded in symbolic mode, with arithmetic turned on.

What to do. Rename the key in any data that happens to use it.

5. number is no longer a type (v4)

In a type annotation, int and float replace the primitive number:

@n : int = 3        -- was: @n : number = 3
@r : float = 0.5

number is now an unresolved type name. A host checker that received {"$type": "number"} receives {"$type": "int"} or {"$type": "float"}.

What does not change

  • The grammar. There are no new operators and no new syntax.
  • A template that uses only integers, and whose context holds only numbers written without a fraction or an exponent, evaluates to the same output.
  • evalProgram and runProgram keep their signatures, apart from the JSON type above. They run without arithmetic.

Arithmetic is separate, and off by default

The nine builtins (sum, product, negate, quotient, inverse, floor-quotient, modulo, floor, real) are an optional profile that a host chooses per evaluation. Without it the names are unbound, so an existing template that binds its own sum or floor keeps working either way: a binding shadows the builtin.

wherehow to turn it on
tramaj-pursrunProgramWith (defaultOptions { arithmetic = true })
tramaj-hsrunProgramWith defaultOptions { optArithmetic = True }
tramaj-clitramaj-cli --arithmetic template.tramaj context.json
playgroundalways on

tramaj-cli analyze arithmetic template.tramaj lists the arithmetic names a template and its libraries reference, without running anything. A host without the profile can use it to refuse a template up front.

Where the rules are written

  • Language reference, sections 3 (values), 5 (number literals), 6 (str), 11 (comparisons and arithmetic) and 13 (the integer range).
  • Node JSON representation, Numbers.
  • Symbols reference, section 1.9 (terms) and 5.3 (reserved keys).
  • decisions.md, section 18, for the reasoning and the alternatives that were rejected.
entry.summary: Numbers are now two types, an integer and a float. This page lists what changes for existing templates and hosts, and what to do about each.

entry.title: Integrating tramaj into a host
entry.content:
Integrating tramaj into a host

Every integration has the same two moving parts, regardless of language:

  1. Evaluate — parse a template and run it against a JSON context to get a Node: the normative, host-agnostic document tree (node-json.md).
  2. Fold — walk that Node and turn it into whatever your host actually renders: real DOM, a UI framework’s virtual tree, another markup language, a config file.

Nothing about Node or the evaluator knows about HTML, a browser, or any particular UI framework (see Properties) — the fold is always something you write for your host, even where this repository already ships one for you. Which of the six paths below applies depends only on what language your host is written in.

The implementations and how they relate: one specification and corpus, six independently written ports, and the folds and CLIs layered on top of two of them.

Host languageGet the NodeWrite the fold
PureScriptdepend on tramaj-purs directlyreuse tramaj-halogen, or write your own
Haskelldepend on tramaj-hs directlywrite your own — none shipped yet
Rustdepend on tramaj-rs directly, or shell out to tramaj-cli-rswrite your own — none shipped yet
JavaScript / TypeScriptdepend on tramaj-js directly, or shell out to tramaj-clireuse tramaj-react, or write your own
Pythondepend on tramaj-py directly, or shell out to python -m tramajwrite your own — none shipped yet
Godepend on tramaj-go directly, or shell out to its tramaj-go CLIwrite your own — none shipped yet
anything elseshell out to tramaj-cli or tramaj-cli-rs, or reimplement the evaluatorwrite your own, over the JSON

Numbers at the boundary

The language has two number types, an integer and a float, and a JSON number is typed by its text: 3 is an integer, 3.0 and 3e0 are floats (reference, section 3). This matters to a host in three places.

  • Reading the context. The host’s JSON parser must keep the difference between 3 and 3.0, and must not round a large integer. JavaScript’s JSON.parse and Haskell’s aeson Value do neither, which is why tramaj-purs and tramaj-hs each ship a Tramaj.Json module with a reader (jsonParser) and a writer (stringify).
  • Reading the result. The output keeps the type: an integer is written as digits and a float always with a fraction or an exponent (node-json.md, Numbers). A fold that renders a scalar child should write it the same way, as str does: tramaj-halogen renders the float 1.0 as 1.0.
  • Choosing whether templates may compute. The nine arithmetic builtins are an optional profile, chosen by the host for each evaluation and off by default. In symbolic mode with the profile on, a result may hold a term, {"$term": "sum", "arguments": [...]}: arithmetic over a symbol, left for the host to evaluate (v3-symbols.md, section 1.9). A host that has not turned the profile on never receives one.
ImplementationTwo number typesArithmetic profileInteger range
tramaj-purs, tramaj-halogen, tramaj-cli, playgroundyesyes-(2^53 - 1) to 2^53 - 1
tramaj-hsyesyessigned 64-bit
tramaj-rs, tramaj-cli-rs, tramaj-js, tramaj-react, tramaj-py, tramaj-gonot yetnot yetevery number is a double

The first two rows are on the main branch and in no release yet. Until the other implementations follow, the same template can give different output on two of them: str(1.0) is 1.0 on the first two rows and 1 on the third. The corpus cases that depend on the split or on arithmetic are marked with "requires", and an implementation that does not declare the name skips them. An existing host moving to the split should read Migrating to integers and floats.

PureScript — import as a library, fold with tramaj-halogen

tramaj-purs, tramaj-halogen, tramaj-cli, and playground are members of one Spago workspace rooted at this repository. A new PureScript package placed as a subdirectory of the workspace, with tramaj-purs (and tramaj-halogen if you’re rendering through Halogen) listed in its spago.yaml dependencies, is picked up by Spago’s workspace discovery with no registry publishing step needed.

The core API:

-- Tramaj.Parser
parseProgram :: String -> Either ParseError Program

-- Tramaj.Eval
runProgram     :: Mode    -> LibraryTable -> Json -> Program -> Either EvalError Json
runProgramWith :: Options -> LibraryTable -> Json -> Program -> Either EvalError Json

type Options = { mode :: Mode, arithmetic :: Boolean }
defaultOptions :: Options   -- { mode: Concrete, arithmetic: false }

-- Tramaj.Json
jsonParser :: String -> Either String Json
stringify  :: Json -> String

Mode is Concrete or Symbolic (v3-symbols.md); LibraryTable supplies whatever the template’s import(...) calls need. Json is Tramaj.Json.Json, not Argonaut’s: a JSON value whose numbers keep their type. Read the context with jsonParser and write the result with stringify; JSON.parse and JSON.stringify cannot tell 3 from 3.0. runProgram runs without the arithmetic profile; runProgramWith (defaultOptions { arithmetic = true }) turns it on. Tramaj.Analysis.deepArithmeticOps reports which arithmetic names a program and its libraries reference, so a host without the profile can refuse one before running it. runProgram gives you the evaluated document as JSON directly, already encoded per node-json.md. If you need the Node value itself rather than its JSON encoding — to fold it without a round-trip through JSON — evalProgramWithEmissions is the lower-level entry point that stops one step earlier.

If your host renders through Halogen, don’t write a fold at all — tramaj-halogen already has one:

-- Tramaj.Halogen
foldToHalogen
  :: forall action slots m
   . (String -> String -> Json -> Maybe action)
  -> Node
  -> Array (ComponentHTML action slots m)

The first argument is a dispatch function: event type, action key, and JSON payload in, an optional host action out. A read-only host supplies \_ _ _ -> Nothing. The result is an Array, not a single element, because a fragment contributes several siblings with no wrapper element. Call validateAttrNames on the Node first — attribute names aren’t validated by the fold itself.

playground/src/Playground/Main.purs is the canonical worked example of the whole pipeline — Tramaj.Parser → Tramaj.Eval → Tramaj.Halogen.foldToHalogen — including dispatchAction, which turns action(...) clicks into real Halogen actions for an interactive host (a read-only host just passes const Nothing instead).

Haskell — the library exists, the fold doesn’t yet

tramaj-hs is an independent Haskell port, built on megaparsec and aeson, that targets the same grammar as the PureScript tramaj-purs and shares its conformance corpus. It’s a normal Cabal library exposing Tramaj.Ast, Tramaj.Parser, Tramaj.Eval, Tramaj.Node, Tramaj.Json, Tramaj.Analysis, and Tramaj.Types — so a Haskell host can depend on it directly (as a source-repository-package or path dependency; it isn’t published to Hackage), the same way a PureScript host depends on tramaj-purs.

What it does not have yet is a tramaj-halogen equivalent — no fold to Lucid, Blaze, or any other Haskell HTML/UI library ships in this repository. A Haskell host gets the parser, the evaluator, and the Node JSON encoding (kept in lockstep with the PureScript Tramaj.Node); writing the fold to your actual rendering library is on you. The shape to follow is tramaj-halogen’s: case on Text/Element/Fragment, recurse into children, and decide what an action(...) payload means in your host.

The evaluator takes and returns Tramaj.Json.Json, a JSON value with separate JInt and JFloat constructors, where it used to take Data.Aeson.Value. jsonParser reads JSON text and types each number by its text; stringify writes it back. fromAeson and toAeson bridge to aeson, with a loss: aeson has already forgotten whether a number was written 3 or 3.0, so fromAeson makes every whole number that fits 64 bits an integer. Integers cover the signed 64-bit range here, wider than the PureScript implementation’s. Arithmetic is off in runProgram and on with runProgramWith defaultOptions {optArithmetic = True}.

Rust — the library exists, plus its own CLI

tramaj-rs is an independent, hand-written Rust port of the same grammar and evaluation semantics as the PureScript tramaj-purs and Haskell tramaj-hs, held to the same shared conformance corpus (corpus/cases/, including v3-symbols.md’s symbols/constraints and v4-types.md’s nominal types, not just the core language; the two number types and arithmetic are not in this port yet, see Numbers at the boundary). It’s a normal Cargo library crate — tramaj_rs::{ast, parser, eval, node, analysis, types} — depended on as a path or git dependency (not published to crates.io yet), the same way a PureScript host depends on tramaj-purs or a Haskell host depends on tramaj-hs:

// tramaj_rs::parser
pub fn parse_program(src: &str) -> Result<Program, ParseError>;

// tramaj_rs::eval
pub fn run_program(
    mode: Mode,
    libs: &LibraryTable,
    ctx: &serde_json::Value,
    program: &Program,
) -> Result<serde_json::Value, EvalError>;

run_program gives you the evaluated result as JSON directly, already encoded per node-json.md when the program produces a document, or the concrete/symbolic envelope from v3-symbols.md §5 otherwise — the same shape runProgram returns on the PureScript and Haskell sides. As with Haskell, there’s no tramaj-halogen equivalent shipped yet: a Rust host gets the parser, evaluator, Node JSON codec, and static analysis, and writes its own fold following the same shape (case on Text/Element/Fragment, recurse into children, decide what an action(...) payload means in your host).

Unlike the Haskell port, Rust also has a tramaj-cli equivalent — tramaj-cli-rs — mirroring tramaj-cli’s command surface field-for-field: the same evaluate/analyze <imports|actions|holes|unsupplied|constraints|symbols|types|card|all> subcommands, the same --lib name=path/--mode concrete|symbolic flags, and the same JSON output shapes. If you’d rather shell out than link a Rust library into your host — including from a non-Rust host — tramaj-cli-rs is an alternative to tramaj-cli with no Node.js runtime required. It does not have tramaj-cli’s --arithmetic flag or analyze arithmetic yet, and it writes a whole-valued float without a fraction.

JavaScript / TypeScript — import as a library, fold with tramaj-react

tramaj-js is an independent, hand-written TypeScript port of the same grammar and evaluation semantics as the PureScript tramaj-purs, Haskell tramaj-hs, and Rust tramaj-rs, held to the same shared conformance corpus (corpus/cases/, including v3-symbols.md’s symbols/constraints and v4-types.md’s nominal types, not just the core language; the two number types and arithmetic are not in this port yet). It’s a normal npm package with no React or DOM dependency — a plain Node or browser host can depend on it the same way a PureScript host depends on tramaj-purs:

// parseProgram, tryParseProgram
function parseProgram(src: string): Program; // throws ParseError

// runProgram
function runProgram(
  mode: Mode,
  libs: LibraryTable,
  ctx: Json,
  program: Program,
): Json; // throws EvalError

Mode is "concrete" or "symbolic" (v3-symbols.md); runProgram gives you the evaluated result as JSON directly, already encoded per node-json.md when the program produces a document, or the concrete/symbolic envelope from v3-symbols.md §5 otherwise — the same shape runProgram returns on the PureScript, Haskell, and Rust sides. evalProgram is the lower-level entry point if you want the Node value itself rather than its JSON encoding, to fold it without a round-trip through JSON.

If your host renders through React, don’t write a fold at all — tramaj-react already has one, the same shape as tramaj-halogen’s:

type Dispatch = (
  event: string,
  key: string,
  payload: Json,
) => MouseEventHandler<Element> | undefined | null;

function foldToReact(dispatch: Dispatch, node: Node): ReactNode[];

dispatch decides which action(...) entries become a real event handler — it inspects the event type itself (foldToReact doesn’t), and returns undefined/null for ones it wants to ignore. Every action a dispatch call accepts is wired to onClick. The result is an array, not a single element, because a fragment contributes several siblings with no wrapper — splice it into your own container, <>{foldToReact(dispatch, node)}</>. Call validateAttrNames on the Node first, same caveat as tramaj-halogen: attribute names aren’t validated by the fold itself.

If you’d rather not add a JS dependency at all — or your host isn’t Node — tramaj-cli (or tramaj-cli-rs) as a subprocess is still the same option open to any other language; see Getting started for the exact CLI invocations, and Any other language below for the general shape of folding its JSON output by hand.

Python — import as a library, standard library only

tramaj-py is an independent, hand-written Python port of the same grammar and evaluation semantics as the other implementations, held to the same shared conformance corpus (corpus/cases/, including v3-symbols.md’s symbols/constraints and v4-types.md’s nominal types; the two number types and arithmetic are not in this port yet). It needs nothing outside the standard library (Python 3.9+), so it drops into a data pipeline, a notebook or a backend service without a Node or PureScript toolchain as a runtime dependency. It’s a normal package — tramaj with ast, parser, evaluator, node, analysis, typesys and jsonval modules, laid out one-to-one like tramaj-js — installed from the repository’s tramaj-py/ directory (not published to PyPI yet):

from tramaj import parse_program, run_program

program = parse_program('.p($ctx.name)')          # raises ParseError
run_program("concrete", {}, {"name": "web"}, program)  # raises EvalError

run_program gives you the evaluated result as plain Python JSON values (dict/list/str/numbers/bool/None), already encoded per node-json.md when the program produces a document, or the concrete/symbolic envelope from v3-symbols.md §5 otherwise — the same shape runProgram returns on every other side. A library table is a dict from import name to parsed program; the mode is "concrete" or "symbolic". eval_program is the lower-level entry point if you want the Node value itself rather than its JSON encoding. Every number is still a double in this port: an exact integer comes back as an int, and str renders as ECMAScript’s Number::toString does. That matches the Rust, JavaScript and Go ports byte-for-byte, and differs from the PureScript and Haskell implementations for a whole-valued float (1 here, 1.0 there).

As with Haskell and Rust, no fold is shipped: a Python host writes its own following the same shape (case on text/element/fragment, recurse into children, decide what an action(...) payload means in your host). Python also has its own tramaj-cli equivalent, python -m tramaj, mirroring tramaj-cli-rs’s evaluate/analyze subcommands, flags and JSON output shapes, so a non-Python host with a Python interpreter around can shell out to it instead of to Node.

Go — import as a module, standard library only

tramaj-go is an independent, hand-written Go port of the same grammar and evaluation semantics as the other implementations, held to the same shared conformance corpus (corpus/cases/, including v3-symbols.md’s symbols/constraints and v4-types.md’s nominal types; the two number types and arithmetic are not in this port yet). It needs nothing outside the standard library (Go 1.21+), so it compiles into a service or a static binary with no Node, Python or PureScript toolchain as a runtime dependency. It’s one package, tramaj, in the repository’s tramaj-go/ directory (no tagged module release yet):

import tramaj "github.com/lucasdicioccio/tramaj/tramaj-go"

program, err := tramaj.ParseProgram(`.p($ctx.name)`) // err is a *tramaj.ParseError
ctx, _ := tramaj.ParseJSON([]byte(`{"name": "web"}`))
out, err := tramaj.RunProgram(tramaj.Concrete, nil, ctx, program) // err is a *tramaj.EvalError
fmt.Println(tramaj.PrettyJSON(out))

RunProgram gives you the evaluated result as a tramaj.JSON value (nil, bool, float64, string, []tramaj.JSON or *tramaj.Object, an object that keeps its keys in order), already encoded per node-json.md when the program produces a document, or the concrete/symbolic envelope from v3-symbols.md §5 otherwise — the same shape runProgram returns on every other side. A library table is a tramaj.Libraries, a map from import name to parsed program; the mode is tramaj.Concrete or tramaj.Symbolic. EvalProgram is the lower-level entry point if you want the *tramaj.Node itself rather than its JSON encoding. Every number is still a float64 in this port, and str renders as ECMAScript’s Number::toString does. That matches the Rust, JavaScript and Python ports byte-for-byte, and differs from the PureScript and Haskell implementations for a whole-valued float (1 here, 1.0 there).

As with Haskell, Rust and Python, no fold is shipped: a Go host writes its own following the same shape (switch on the node’s Type, recurse into Children, decide what an action attribute means in your host). Go also has its own tramaj-cli equivalent, tramaj-go (go build ./cmd/tramaj-go), mirroring tramaj-cli-rs’s evaluate/analyze subcommands, flags and JSON output shapes.

Any other language

For a host in a language with no PureScript, Haskell, Rust, JavaScript, Python or Go interop story — Java, C#, whatever — there are two options:

(a) Full reimplementation. Port the parser and evaluator to your language, the way tramaj-hs ports the PureScript original. Worth it only if you need to evaluate templates natively (e.g. embedding evaluation in a process that can’t shell out, or needs it to run in-process for performance). reference.md is the full grammar and evaluation semantics to implement against, and the conformance corpus (corpus/cases/ in the repository — template + context + expected output triples) is what the six existing implementations are held to; a new implementation should be checked against the same corpus.

(b) Partial implementation, starting from tramaj-cli’s output. For most hosts this is the pragmatic choice: don’t reimplement the parser or evaluator at all. Shell out to tramaj-cli:

tramaj-cli template.tramaj context.json
tramaj-cli --arithmetic template.tramaj context.json   # with the arithmetic builtins

which prints the evaluated Node as JSON on stdout, exactly per node-json.md. In that JSON 3 is an integer and 3.0 a float; a host that needs the difference reads it with a parser that keeps it. Your host only needs to write the fold — parse that JSON, case on whether each node is text, an element, or a fragment, recurse into children, and decide what each element’s action(...) entries mean in your host — the same shape as tramaj-halogen’s fold, just written against decoded JSON instead of a native Node value. tramaj-cli’s analyze subcommands (imports/actions/holes/unsupplied/constraints/symbols/arithmetic/types) are available the same way, without a context file, if your host wants the static-analysis facts from Properties rather than a rendered document.

This is also the fastest way to prototype an integration in any language before deciding whether a full reimplementation is ever worth it.

See the Roadmap for what a new implementation needs to cover and where to start if you want to build one; Rust, JavaScript, Python and Go each have one now (tramaj-rs, tramaj-js, tramaj-py and tramaj-go, above).
entry.summary: Six ways to embed tramaj in a host, depending on your language: import the library, or work from tramaj-cli's JSON output.

entry.title: Getting started with tramaj
entry.content:
Getting started with tramaj

This is a practical walkthrough. For the language’s core ideas, see the overview on the home page; for the full grammar, see the Reference.

A template can be run in four places, and each section below covers one:

The fastest way in: the playground

Before installing anything, try the playground — it runs entirely in the browser, needs no setup, and shows the same panels described below (evaluated AST, rendered HTML, action log).

Installing the toolchain

tramaj’s PureScript packages are one Spago workspace. You need purs and spago on your PATH:

npm install -g purescript spago

Anything that bundles a browser or Node bundle — the playground and the CLI — also needs esbuild, which is a devDependency of the repo root:

git clone https://github.com/lucasdicioccio/tramaj.git
cd tramaj
npm install
export PATH="$PWD/node_modules/.bin:$PATH"

Writing a first template

Create hello.tramaj:

@n=cardinality($ctx.items)
.p("there are `$n` item(s)")

and a context to evaluate it against, hello.json:

{"items": ["a", "b", "c"]}

Running it

spago run -p tramaj-cli --args "hello.tramaj hello.json"

This prints the evaluated Node AST as JSON — a p element wrapping the text there are 3 item(s). See node-json.md for what that JSON shape means, or fold it into real HTML by rendering it through a host like tramaj-halogen.

Computing with numbers

A number is an integer or a float, decided by how it is written: 3 is an integer, 3.0 and 3e0 are floats. That holds for a literal in the template and for a number in the context file. The two types do not mix: eq(3, 3.0) is false, and gt(1.5, 0) is an error that gt(1.5, 0.0) fixes.

There are no operators. Arithmetic is nine named builtins: sum, product, negate, quotient, inverse, floor-quotient, modulo, floor and real. Create bill.tramaj:

@subtotal = sum($ctx.compute, $ctx.storage, negate($ctx.credit))
@share    = branch(0, gt($ctx.total, 0),
                   floor-quotient(product(100, $ctx.used), $ctx.total))
.p("subtotal `$subtotal`, `$share`% used")

and bill.json:

{"compute": 120, "storage": 30, "credit": 25, "used": 3, "total": 8}

Arithmetic is a profile the host turns on. With the CLI that is the --arithmetic flag:

spago run -p tramaj-cli --args "--arithmetic bill.tramaj bill.json"

The result is a p element with the text subtotal 125, 37% used. Without the flag the nine names are unbound, and the CLI says which ones the template uses. sum and product take all integers or all floats, never a mix; real(x) and floor(x) convert, and each accepts both types.

The playground runs with arithmetic on and has an arithmetic-demo tab. Numbers used to be a single type: if you have templates written before the split, read Migrating to integers and floats. The split and arithmetic are in the PureScript and Haskell implementations; the Rust, JavaScript, Python and Go ones do not have them yet.

Splitting a template into libraries

A template can import(...) another template as a library. Pass each one with --lib name=path:

spago run -p tramaj-cli --args "--lib greeter=greeter.tramaj hello.tramaj hello.json"

Repeat --lib for as many libraries as the template’s imports need.

Inspecting a template without running it

Because imports, action keys, and context reads are all static positions (see Properties), the CLI can answer questions about a template without a context file at all:

node tramaj-cli/dist/tramaj-cli.js analyze imports hello.tramaj
node tramaj-cli/dist/tramaj-cli.js analyze actions hello.tramaj
node tramaj-cli/dist/tramaj-cli.js analyze holes hello.tramaj
node tramaj-cli/dist/tramaj-cli.js analyze unsupplied hello.tramaj
node tramaj-cli/dist/tramaj-cli.js analyze arithmetic bill.tramaj
node tramaj-cli/dist/tramaj-cli.js analyze all hello.tramaj

(These need a bundled CLI first: spago bundle -p tramaj-cli --platform node --outfile dist/tramaj-cli.js, run from tramaj-cli/.)

Embedding in a real host

Running templates from the command line is one thing; wiring them into an actual application is another — see Integrating tramaj for the four paths (PureScript, Haskell, JavaScript, or any other language) and what each one actually looks like.

Where to go next

  • Use cases for where this fits alongside other templating approaches.
  • Reference for the full grammar, builtins, and the v3/v4 extensions.
  • Integrating tramaj for embedding it in a host application.
  • Migrating to integers and floats if you have templates or a host written before numbers became two types.
  • For coding agents if you’re setting an LLM loose on tramaj templates rather than writing them by hand.
entry.summary: Write a first template, run it, and see where to go from there.

entry.title: tramaj for coding agents
entry.content:
tramaj for coding agents

tramaj was designed to be as easy for a model to emit correctly as for a person to write by hand — a small builtin set, one expression grammar, and no template/expression phase split to keep track of. This page is a dense cheatsheet plus a fetch strategy for getting the full grammar when the summary below isn’t enough.

Fetch the canonical source first

Don’t rely on prose alone for anything you’re about to emit — pull the normative text:

  • Every page on this site is also served as plain text at /text/<page-name>.cmark.text (e.g. /text/reference-language.cmark.text) — no HTML to strip.
  • The specs themselves are the ultimate source of truth, on GitHub: reference.md, node-json.md, v3-symbols.md, v4-types.md.
  • corpus/cases/ in the repository is a conformance corpus: each case is a template.tramaj + ctx.json + expected.json triple (plus optional libs/*.tramaj) that every implementation must satisfy — treat these as runnable, ground-truth examples rather than prose. A case’s meta.json may carry "requires" (int-float, arithmetic, …), naming a feature an implementation must declare before it runs that case.
  • See also llms.txt for a short machine-readable index of the above (Kitchen-Sink serves arbitrary .txt files under /raw/, so this isn’t at the conventional /llms.txt root path).

Leaders — what each sigil means

LeaderMeaning
.document: .tag(...) element, or .(...) fragment
$read a binding or path
@define a binding (@name=expr)
!emit a constraint, statement position (!constraint(name, ...))
?symbolic allocation/demand, v3 (?(key))
%type hole, v4
--line comment, to end of line

Shape of a program

@n=cardinality($ctx.items)
.p("there are `$n` item(s)")

An optional block of @name=expr bindings, evaluated once each in order, followed by one root expression. Backtick-quoted `$expr` interpolates into a string; a bare $path can be a child directly. a <> b concatenates strings, arrays, and objects.

Documents are ordinary values

There is no separate “template value” type — an element or fragment can be bound, passed to a function, and returned from one:

@kids=.(.p("one"), .p("two"))
@panel=(title, children) => .section(.h2($title), $children)

.main($panel("Deployment", $kids))

Numbers and arithmetic

Two number types, told apart by the text of the literal or of the JSON number in the context. Nothing converts between them implicitly.

writtentypestr gives
3, -7, 1_000_000integer3, -7, 1000000
3.0, 1.5, 1e5float3.0, 1.5, 100000.0
  • eq(1, 1.0) is false. lt/lte/gt/gte take two integers or two floats; a mixed pair is a TypeMismatch. Write gt($x, 0.0) for a float.
  • There are no operators: no +, -, *, /. Arithmetic is nine named builtins, and there is no subtraction: sum(a, negate(b)).
builtinoperandsresult
sum(…), product(…)one or more, all integers or all floats; arrays are flattenedsame type
negate(x)integer or floatsame type
quotient(a, b), inverse(x)floats onlyfloat
floor-quotient(a, b), modulo(a, b)integers onlyinteger, rounding toward negative infinity
floor(x)eitherinteger
real(x)eitherfloat
@subtotal = sum($ctx.compute, $ctx.storage, negate($ctx.credit))
@share    = branch(0, gt($ctx.total, 0),
                   floor-quotient(product(100, $ctx.used), $ctx.total))
@total    = sum(0.0, map($ctx.lines,
                         (l) => product(real($l.qty), real($l.price))))
  • A mixed call (sum(1, 2.5), quotient(1, 2)) is a TypeMismatch. When the type of a context number is not known, normalize it: real($x) or floor($x).
  • sum() and sum([]) are a TypeMismatch. Seed a fold over a list that may be empty: sum(0, $xs) or sum(0.0, $xs).
  • A zero divisor, an integer overflow and a non-finite float are a NotRepresentable error, never null or 0. Guard with branch, whose unselected arm is not evaluated.
  • Arithmetic is a profile the host turns on (tramaj-cli --arithmetic). Without it the nine names are unbound.
  • In symbolic mode, a builtin with a symbol among its operands evaluates to a term, {"$term": "sum", "arguments": [...]}, for the host to evaluate. "$term" is a reserved object key, like "$sym" and "$type".
  • The type primitives are int and float (@n : int = 3); there is no number.

Do not emit round, sort-by, sort-by-descending or format-number: they are specified in the reference, marked [§20], and no implementation has them yet. The number split and the nine builtins above are in the PureScript and Haskell implementations, and not yet in the Rust, JavaScript, Python and Go ones, where every number is still a double. Templates written before the split: Migrating to integers and floats.

Actions are opaque to the language

action("on-click", "select", {"id": $i.id}) attaches structured data to an element. The language does not interpret it — a host decides what the key means. Action keys and adaptation prefixes must be literal strings, never computed, which is what keeps “what actions can this template emit” statically answerable.

Imports

import(...) pulls in another program as a library. Parameters can arrive as an expression, as a ctx(path) hole (a static marker that the importing program’s own context gets read at that point), or be omitted and supplied later by calling the import. Imports are lazy — nothing runs until .rendered or .vals is read on the result.

v3 — symbols and constraints (frozen, implemented)

?(key) allocates an opaque symbol; only the root program may do this (libraries raise AllocationInLibrary). !constraint(name, ...) emits a constraint. Running in Symbolic mode (a host choice, not something the template declares) wraps the result in a tramaj/symbolic/1 envelope of root value, symbols, and constraints instead of a finished document — use this when the actual values should come from a solver rather than be supplied up front. Full grammar: v3-symbols.md.

v4 — types (draft, implemented)

@x : T = e desugars to @x=e plus a has-type constraint carrying T’s canonical id. Types are resolved and erased before evaluation — tramaj fixes type identity (canonical ids, string equality), a separate host checker decides whether values actually satisfy it. Type parameters thread through imports. Full grammar: v4-types.md.

Static analyses available without evaluating

Because imports, action keys, adaptation prefixes, and ctx(...) paths are all literal strings in the syntax, these can all be answered by walking the AST — no context, no evaluation:

  • what a program imports, and with what parameters
  • what actions it can possibly emit
  • what context paths it reads (ctx(...) holes)
  • which import parameters are still unsupplied
  • which arithmetic builtins it references (analyze arithmetic)
  • (v3/v4) what constraints and symbols/types it introduces

tramaj-cli’s analyze subcommand exposes these directly — see Getting started for exact invocations. If you’re generating a template and want to self-check it before handing it to a host, running analyze on it is cheaper and more reliable than re-deriving these properties by re-reading your own output.

Common pitfalls

  • Don’t compute an import name, action key, or ctx(...) path from an expression — these must be literal strings; the grammar doesn’t allow otherwise.
  • Bindings are visible only after their declaration, in order — not mutually recursive.
  • A library (something loaded via import) may not call ?(key) — only the root program may allocate symbols.
  • Don’t compare or combine an integer with a float: gt($ratio, 0) fails when $ratio is a float. Match the literal to the value, or convert with real/floor.
  • Don’t write a count as 1.0 or 1e3: a float renders with its fraction (1.0, 1000.0).
  • Evaluation order is unconstrained outside of binding precedence: don’t write templates that rely on side-effect ordering, because there isn’t one — evaluation is meant to be referentially transparent.
entry.summary: A dense syntax reference and fetch strategy for an LLM or agent emitting tramaj templates.
